q: In the Henry system of primary classification, what value is given to a whorl on the right thumb or the right index finger?
r: Fingers 1 and 2 (right thumb and right index) carry a whorl value of 16.
A value of 8 is given to fingers 3 and 4.
A value of 4 is given to fingers 5 and 6.
No finger has a value of 32; 32 is the highest possible sum including the added 1.
e: Whorl values are 16 for fingers 1-2, 8 for 3-4, 4 for 5-6, 2 for 7-8 and 1 for 9-10.

q: Which branch of forensic science identifies persons through their teeth and bite marks?
a: Forensic odontology
Forensic anthropology
Forensic serology
Dactyloscopy
r: Forensic odontology applies dental science to identification and bite mark analysis.
Forensic anthropology studies skeletal remains.
Forensic serology studies blood and other body fluids.
Dactyloscopy is the study of fingerprints.
e: Dental records are compared with the teeth of unidentified remains.

q: Why does the Henry primary classification have 1,024 possible combinations?
a: Because the numerator and denominator can each range from 1 to 32
Because each of the ten fingers can have one of 1,024 patterns
Because the FBI added 1,024 new pattern types to the system
Because every fingerprint card is given its own serial number
r: Adding 1 to the sums of whorl values makes each part range from 1 to 32, so there are 32 x 32 = 1,024 combinations.
Fingers do not have 1,024 pattern types.
The number comes from the formula, not from added pattern types.
Serial numbers have nothing to do with the primary classification.
e: The 1 is added so that the formula never has a zero, and the primary is always at least 1 over 1.

q: Why can DNA profiling not tell identical twins apart?
a: Because identical twins develop from one zygote and share the same nuclear DNA
Because identical twins have no DNA in their blood cells
Because DNA can only be taken from adults, not from twins
Because the DNA of twins changes after birth
r: Identical twins come from a single fertilized egg, so their nuclear DNA profiles are the same; fingerprints, however, differ.
Twins have DNA in their nucleated cells like anyone else.
DNA can be taken from persons of any age.
DNA does not change after birth in a way that separates twins.
e: Fingerprints are one way to distinguish identical twins, because ridge details form differently in each.

q: Why are fingerprint cards filed according to their classification formulas?
a: So that a card can be found by its formula without searching all the cards
So that only cards of persons with criminal records are kept
So that cards are arranged by the date the prints were taken
So that the names of the persons can be kept secret
r: Filing by classification groups cards with the same formula, which allows a search to be narrowed quickly.
Filing method does not decide whose cards are kept.
Date-based filing would force a search of every card.
Filing by formula is about retrieval, not secrecy.
e: Name files are kept separately so that a card can also be found by name.

q: Why are teeth especially useful for identifying victims of fires and mass disasters?
a: They resist heat and decay, and can be compared with dental records
They regrow after death and show the person's recent meals
They carry the person's name and birth date inside the enamel
They are identical in all members of the same family
r: Teeth are the hardest tissue of the body and survive fire and decomposition; their features can be matched with dental charts and X-rays.
Teeth do not regrow after death.
Teeth do not carry names or dates.
Teeth differ between family members; that is why they help identify individuals.
e: Forensic odontology is a standard method in disaster victim identification.

q: A fingerprint pattern has one delta, and its ridges enter, recurve and leave on the side toward the little finger. What is the pattern?
a: Ulnar loop
Radial loop
Plain whorl
Tented arch
r: A loop whose ridges flow toward the little finger (ulna side) is an ulnar loop.
A radial loop flows toward the thumb (radius side).
A whorl has at least two deltas.
A tented arch has no recurving ridge with a ridge count.
e: Loops are the most common fingerprint pattern.

q: A pattern has two deltas, and a line drawn between the deltas cuts across the circular ridges of the inner area. What is the pattern?
a: Plain whorl
Central pocket loop whorl
Double loop whorl
Accidental whorl
r: A plain whorl has two deltas and at least one ridge making a complete circuit, and the line between the deltas touches or crosses a recurving ridge in the inner area.
In a central pocket loop whorl, the line between the deltas does not touch any recurving ridge in the inner area.
A double loop whorl has two separate loop formations.
An accidental whorl combines two or more different patterns or fits no other type.
e: The imaginary line between the deltas separates the plain whorl from the central pocket loop.

q: Ridges enter from one side, rise slightly in the middle, and flow out the other side, with no delta. What is the pattern?
a: Plain arch
Tented arch
Radial loop
Accidental whorl
r: A plain arch has ridges flowing from one side to the other with a gentle rise, and no delta.
A tented arch has an angle, an upthrust, or an incomplete loop in the center.
A loop needs a delta and a recurving ridge.
A whorl needs at least two deltas.
e: Arches are the least common of the basic patterns.

q: A latent print recorded years ago is matched to a suspect arrested today. Which principle of fingerprint identification makes this possible?
a: Permanence: ridge details do not change during a person's life
Variation: ridge details change every few years
Classification: all fingerprints can be grouped into one pattern
Similarity: prints of relatives are always the same
r: Friction ridge details form before birth and stay the same until decomposition, barring permanent scars.
Ridge details do not change over time.
Classification helps filing but does not explain identification over time.
Relatives do not have identical prints.
e: The principles are individuality, permanence, and classifiable general patterns.

q: A latent print and a suspect's inked print are both ulnar loops, but their ridge endings and bifurcations are in different positions. What should the examiner conclude?
a: They are not from the same finger, because identity rests on ridge details
They are from the same finger, because the patterns match
They are from the same person, but from different fingers
No conclusion is possible, because loops are too common
r: The pattern is only a class characteristic; identity depends on ridge characteristics agreeing in kind and relative position.
A matching pattern type alone does not prove identity.
Different ridge details show the print did not come from that finger; nothing shows which finger it came from.
An examiner can exclude a source when the ridge details clearly disagree.
e: Ridge characteristics include ridge endings, bifurcations, dots, short ridges and enclosures.

q: A pattern has a delta and a recurving ridge, but no ridge crosses the line between the delta and the core. How is it classified?
a: Tented arch, because a loop needs a ridge count of at least one
Ulnar loop, because a recurving ridge is present
Plain whorl, because there is a delta
Plain arch, because it has a delta
r: A loop requires a sufficient recurve, a delta, and a ridge count of at least one across a looping ridge; without the ridge count it is a tented arch.
A recurve alone is not enough to make a loop.
A whorl needs two deltas.
A plain arch has no delta.
e: Patterns that lack one of the essentials of a loop are commonly classified as tented arches.

q: When taking rolled fingerprint impressions, how should the fingers be rolled?
a: Thumbs toward the subject's body; other fingers away from it
All fingers toward the subject's body
All fingers away from the subject's body
Thumbs and fingers pressed flat without rolling
r: Thumbs are rolled toward the body and the fingers away from it, which uses the natural movement of the hand and gives a clear nail-to-nail impression.
Rolling all fingers toward the body is awkward and tends to smudge.
Thumbs are rolled toward the body, not away from it.
Flat impressions are taken separately; rolled impressions require rolling.
e: Rolled impressions record the full friction ridge area from nail edge to nail edge.

q: After rolling each finger, the technician also presses the four fingers of each hand together on the card, then both thumbs. Why?
a: To check that the rolled prints are in the correct finger order
To replace the rolled prints if they are clear
To record the palm prints of the subject
To find out whether the subject is right- or left-handed
r: Plain (simultaneous) impressions let the examiner verify the sequence of the rolled impressions.
The plain impressions supplement, not replace, the rolled ones.
Palm prints are taken on a separate card.
Handedness is not determined from plain impressions.
e: Errors in finger order would give a wrong classification formula.

q: A threatening letter on ordinary paper is suspected to bear latent prints. Which method is most suitable?
a: Ninhydrin
Black powder dusting
Cyanoacrylate fuming
Small particle reagent
r: Ninhydrin reacts with amino acids absorbed in porous surfaces like paper, producing a purple color.
Powders work best on smooth, non-porous surfaces.
Cyanoacrylate fuming is used mainly on non-porous surfaces such as plastic and glass.
Small particle reagent is used on wet, non-porous surfaces.
e: The method of development depends on the surface: porous, non-porous or semi-porous.

q: A latent print is visible on a drinking glass from the crime scene. Which method is appropriate?
a: Dusting with powder, then lifting with tape
Spraying with ninhydrin solution
Soaking in silver nitrate solution
Treating with iodine fumes on paper
r: Fingerprint powders adhere to the oily residue on smooth, non-porous surfaces like glass; the print is photographed and lifted.
Ninhydrin is for porous surfaces like paper.
Silver nitrate is for porous surfaces.
Iodine fuming is mainly for porous surfaces and gives temporary results.
e: Prints should be photographed before lifting.

q: The fingers of a body recovered from the water are badly wrinkled. What should be done to obtain readable prints?
a: Inject a tissue builder under the skin to restore the ridges
Dust the fingers with black powder and lift with tape
Treat the fingers with ninhydrin and wait one day
Take only the palm prints and leave the fingers
r: Injecting a tissue builder, such as glycerin, under the skin fills out wrinkled fingertips so ridges can be recorded.
Powder and tape do not restore wrinkled ridges.
Ninhydrin is for latent prints on porous surfaces, not for restoring skin.
The fingers can still be recorded after restoration; palms are not a substitute.
e: Other post-mortem techniques include boiling or peeling the skin for decomposed bodies, done by trained personnel.

q: Why must a developed latent print be photographed before it is lifted?
a: Lifting may damage it; the photo keeps its original look and location
Photographing the print makes the lifting tape stick better
A photo is needed only when the print is on paper
Photographs replace the need to lift the print in all cases
r: A lift can fail or distort the print; a photograph with a scale preserves the print as found and documents where it was.
Photography does not affect the adhesion of the tape.
Prints on any surface should be photographed.
The lift is often still taken; the photo is an added safeguard.
e: Documentation is a basic rule in preserving physical evidence.

q: An examiner places a latent print and an inked print side by side and checks whether their ridge details agree. Which phase of ACE-V is this?
a: Comparison
Analysis
Evaluation
Verification
r: Comparison is the side-by-side examination of the latent and known prints.
Analysis studies the latent print alone to judge its quality and features.
Evaluation is reaching a conclusion from the comparison.
Verification is an independent check by another examiner.
e: ACE-V stands for Analysis, Comparison, Evaluation and Verification.

q: After an examiner identifies a latent print, a second qualified examiner independently repeats the examination. Which phase of ACE-V is this?
a: Verification
Analysis
Comparison
Evaluation
r: Verification is the independent re-examination by another qualified examiner.
Analysis is the first study of the latent print.
Comparison is the side-by-side examination.
Evaluation is the first examiner's conclusion.
e: Verification guards against errors by a single examiner.

q: What is the approximate speed of light in a vacuum?
a: 300,000 kilometers per second
30,000 kilometers per second
3,000 kilometers per second
3,000,000 kilometers per second
r: Light travels at about 300,000 km (186,000 miles) per second in a vacuum.
30,000 km/s is ten times too slow.
3,000 km/s is a hundred times too slow.
3,000,000 km/s is ten times too fast.
e: Light is a form of electromagnetic energy that travels in straight lines.

q: What range of wavelengths makes up the visible light that the human eye can see?
a: About 400 to 700 nanometers
About 10 to 100 nanometers
About 1 to 10 millimeters
About 1 to 10 kilometers
r: Visible light ranges from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red).
Below 400 nm is ultraviolet and beyond; 10-100 nm is far ultraviolet.
Millimeter waves are microwaves.
Kilometer waves are radio waves.
e: Ultraviolet and infrared light, just outside this range, are used in forensic photography.

q: If the distance between the flash and the subject is doubled, what happens to the light falling on the subject?
a: It becomes one-fourth as strong
It becomes one-half as strong
It stays the same
It becomes twice as strong
r: By the inverse square law, light intensity varies inversely with the square of the distance: 1 / 2 squared = 1/4.
One-half would be true only if light fell off in direct proportion to distance.
Light weakens with distance.
Light does not get stronger with distance.
e: The inverse square law explains why subjects far from the flash look dark.

q: Why does a photographer use bounce flash by aiming the flash at a white ceiling?
a: To spread softer light and reduce harsh shadows
To make the flash travel faster to the subject
To increase the depth of field of the lens
To make the photograph appear in black and white
r: Bouncing light off a large surface diffuses it, giving more even lighting with softer shadows.
The speed of light does not change.
Depth of field depends on aperture, focal length and distance.
Bounce flash does not change color into black and white.
e: A colored ceiling can tint the light, so a white surface is preferred.

q: Why is oblique lighting used to photograph a footwear impression in dust?
a: The low-angle light creates shadows that show the relief of the impression
The light from above removes all shadows from the impression
The light changes the color of the dust so it shows better
The light makes the impression larger in the photograph
r: Light from a low angle across the surface casts shadows in the depressions, revealing detail.
Light from directly above flattens the image and hides relief.
Oblique light does not change the dust's color.
Lighting does not change the size of the impression.
e: The light should be moved around the impression to find the angle that shows most detail.

q: A light ray bends as it passes at an angle from air into a glass lens. What property of light is this?
a: Refraction
Reflection
Absorption
Diffusion
r: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium to another of different density; lenses work by refraction.
Reflection is light bouncing off a surface.
Absorption is light being taken in by a material.
Diffusion is the scattering of light by a rough or translucent surface.
e: The ability of lenses to form images depends on refraction.

q: A photographer needs the whole crime scene sharp, from the nearest to the farthest object. What setting should he use?
a: A small aperture, such as f/16
A wide aperture, such as f/2
A faster shutter speed only
A higher ISO only
r: A small aperture (large f-number) gives a greater depth of field.
A wide aperture gives a shallow depth of field.
Shutter speed controls motion blur, not depth of field.
ISO controls sensitivity, not depth of field.
e: A small aperture lets in less light, so a slower shutter speed or tripod may be needed.

q: A photographer must freeze the motion of a moving vehicle at a scene. What should he adjust?
a: Use a fast shutter speed, such as 1/500 second
Use a slow shutter speed, such as 1 second
Use the smallest aperture available
Use the lowest ISO available
r: A fast shutter speed stops motion.
A slow shutter speed blurs moving subjects.
A small aperture increases depth of field but reduces light, often forcing a slower shutter.
A low ISO reduces sensitivity, which also tends to force a slower shutter.
e: The exposure triangle links aperture, shutter speed and ISO.

q: The camera is on a tripod, the scene is still and dim, and the photographer wants low noise and great depth of field. What should he adjust?
a: Use a longer shutter speed
Use a much higher ISO
Use the widest aperture
Hold the camera by hand instead
r: With a tripod and a still scene, a long exposure collects enough light while keeping a low ISO and a small aperture.
A high ISO adds noise.
A wide aperture reduces depth of field.
Holding the camera by hand during a long exposure causes blur.
e: Time exposures are useful for night scenes and low light.

q: Upon arriving at a crime scene, which photographs should be taken first?
a: Overall views that show the entire scene
Close-ups of each item with a scale
Mid-range views of the most important evidence
Photographs of the suspects at the station
r: Overall (establishing) views record the scene as a whole before anything is disturbed.
Close-ups come after the overall and mid-range views.
Mid-range views follow the overall views.
Suspects are photographed separately, not as part of the first scene photographs.
e: The usual sequence is overall, mid-range, then close-up photographs.

q: A bullet hole in a wall must be photographed for later measurement. Which procedure is correct?
a: Keep the camera square to the wall; take one shot without and one with a scale
Take one angled shot with a scale placed across the hole itself
Take one shot without a scale so the hole is not covered
Take the shot from a distance with a wide-angle lens
r: The camera back should be parallel to the surface to avoid distortion, and the evidence is photographed first without and then with a scale.
An angled view distorts measurements, and the scale must not cover the evidence.
A photo with a scale is needed for measurement.
A distant wide-angle shot does not show the hole in usable detail.
e: The photo without a scale shows that nothing was hidden by the scale.

q: A correct exposure is f/8 at 1/125 second. The photographer changes to f/11. Which shutter speed keeps the same exposure?
a: 1/60 second
1/250 second
1/500 second
1/125 second
r: f/11 lets in half the light of f/8, so the shutter must stay open twice as long: 1/60.
1/250 would halve the light again, underexposing by two stops.
1/500 would underexpose by three stops.
Keeping 1/125 would underexpose by one stop.
e: Each full f-stop or shutter-speed step doubles or halves the light.

q: Why must the crime scene be photographed before any evidence is moved?
a: Photos record the original condition, which cannot be restored once disturbed
Moving evidence first makes the photos clearer
Photos are needed only for evidence that will be destroyed
Evidence must be moved first so the scale can be placed
r: Photographs are a permanent record of the scene as found; once items are moved, the original positions are lost.
Moving evidence first destroys the record of its position.
All evidence and the scene as a whole are photographed.
Scales are placed next to evidence without moving it, after photos without scale.
e: Courts rely on scene photographs to understand positions and relationships of evidence.

q: A photographer raises the ISO from 100 to 3200 to avoid using flash in a dark room. What is the main trade-off?
a: More digital noise, which reduces fine detail
Less depth of field in the photograph
More motion blur in the photograph
A permanent change in the lens focal length
r: Higher ISO increases sensitivity but adds noise, which can hide fine detail in evidence.
Depth of field depends on aperture, not ISO.
Higher ISO allows faster shutter speeds, which reduces blur.
ISO does not affect focal length.
e: Each setting in the exposure triangle has a trade-off.

q: Which lens is best for photographing a small toolmark at life size?
a: Macro lens
Wide-angle lens
Telephoto lens
Fisheye lens
r: A macro lens focuses very close and can reproduce small objects at 1:1.
A wide-angle lens covers a broad view and distorts close subjects.
A telephoto lens magnifies distant subjects.
A fisheye lens produces strong distortion.
e: Macro photography is used for fingerprints, toolmarks and small items.

q: A photographer must capture an entire small room from the doorway. Which lens is most suitable?
a: Wide-angle lens
Telephoto lens
Macro lens
Long zoom lens
r: A wide-angle lens has a short focal length and a wide angle of view.
A telephoto lens has a narrow view.
A macro lens is for close-ups.
A long zoom set at its long end gives a narrow view.
e: Wide-angle lenses can distort straight lines near the edges.

q: Evidence lies across a river that the photographer cannot cross yet. Which lens is most suitable?
a: Telephoto lens
Wide-angle lens
Macro lens
Normal lens
r: A telephoto lens magnifies distant subjects.
A wide-angle lens makes distant objects look smaller.
A macro lens is for very close subjects.
A normal lens does not magnify distant subjects enough.
e: Telephoto lenses have long focal lengths and a narrow angle of view.

q: Photos of people walking at a scene come out blurred. Which camera setting should be changed first?
a: Shutter speed
Aperture
White balance
Focus mode
r: The shutter controls how long the sensor is exposed; a faster speed freezes motion.
Aperture controls the amount of light and depth of field.
White balance controls color, not blur.
Focus mode affects sharpness of still subjects, not motion blur.
e: Motion blur comes from movement during the exposure.

q: Why is a wide-angle lens not ideal for close-up photographs used to measure evidence?
a: It distorts shapes, especially near the edges of the frame
It cannot focus on any object closer than ten meters
It lets in no light unless a flash is used
It records the image only in black and white
r: Wide-angle lenses exaggerate perspective and bend lines near the edges, which affects measurements.
Wide-angle lenses can focus at close distances.
Wide-angle lenses let in light like other lenses.
The lens does not decide color or black and white.
e: Normal or macro lenses with the camera square to the surface are used for measurements.

q: Why is a lens with a focal length near the diagonal of the film or sensor called a normal lens?
a: It gives a perspective close to what the human eye sees
It is the only lens that can be used with a flash
It has the widest view of all lenses
It produces no light falloff at any aperture
r: A focal length close to the diagonal of the format, such as 50 mm on full frame, gives a natural perspective.
Any lens can be used with a flash.
Wide-angle lenses have wider views.
All lenses show some falloff at certain apertures.
e: Normal lenses are useful for mid-range photographs that show evidence as people see it.

q: In a suspected poisoning death, what is the main role of forensic toxicology?
a: To identify and measure poisons or drugs in body samples
To identify the suspect by examining his fingerprints
To determine the time of death from the body temperature
To examine the handwriting on any suicide note
r: Toxicology analyzes blood, urine and tissues for drugs and poisons and interprets whether they caused or contributed to death.
Fingerprints are examined in dactyloscopy.
Time of death is estimated by forensic medicine.
Handwriting is examined in questioned document examination.
e: Toxicology results are interpreted together with autopsy findings.

q: Why is an unbroken chain of custody important in forensic chemistry cases?
a: It shows the item examined is the same item seized, unchanged
It allows the chemist to skip the confirmatory test
It lets the police keep the evidence at home
It makes the evidence admissible without a chemist's report
r: The chain of custody accounts for each person who handled the item, proving its identity and integrity.
The chain of custody does not replace testing.
Evidence must be kept in proper custody, not at home.
The chemist's findings are still needed to prove what the item is.
e: In drug cases, gaps in the chain of custody have led to acquittals.
l: R.A. 9165, Sec. 21, as amended by R.A. 10640

q: How does a preliminary (presumptive) test differ from a confirmatory test?
a: A presumptive test only suggests presence; a confirmatory test identifies it
A presumptive test is done in court; a confirmatory test at the scene
A presumptive test is always more accurate than a confirmatory one
A presumptive test needs no sample; a confirmatory test needs one
r: Presumptive tests are quick screening tests that can give false positives; confirmatory tests specifically identify the substance.
Both are done in the field or laboratory, not in court.
Confirmatory tests are more specific and reliable.
Both tests need a sample.
e: Examples: Kastle-Meyer (presumptive for blood); Takayama and Teichmann crystal tests (confirmatory for blood).

q: A reddish stain on a shirt turns pink with the Kastle-Meyer (phenolphthalein) test. What is the proper next step?
a: Do a confirmatory test, such as a crystal test, before calling it blood
Report the stain as human blood based on the color change alone
Discard the shirt because the test has used up the stain
Report the stain as rust because it is reddish
r: Kastle-Meyer is presumptive; a confirmatory test such as Takayama or Teichmann, then a test for human origin, is needed.
A presumptive result does not prove blood, and it says nothing about human origin.
The rest of the stain must be preserved for further tests.
The test result suggests blood, not rust.
e: The precipitin test determines whether blood is of human origin.

q: A blood-soaked shirt is recovered from a crime scene. How should it be packaged?
a: Air-dry it at room temperature, then pack it in a paper bag
Seal it while wet in an airtight plastic bag
Wash it to remove dirt before sending it to the laboratory
Dry it under direct sunlight to speed up drying
r: Air-drying and paper packaging prevent mold and bacteria from destroying the biological evidence.
Sealing wet items in plastic traps moisture and promotes decay.
Washing destroys the evidence.
Direct sunlight and heat can degrade DNA.
e: Each item is packaged separately to avoid cross-contamination.

q: Known hair samples must be taken from a suspect for comparison. Which procedure is correct?
a: Pull or comb hairs from different areas of the scalp, roots included
Cut a few hairs from one spot near the neck using scissors
Pick one hair from the suspect's comb at home
Ask the suspect to bring any hair he chooses
r: Known samples should represent the whole scalp, and pulled hairs with roots allow DNA testing.
Cut hairs lack roots and represent only one area.
A single hair from a comb may not be the suspect's and does not represent variation.
The suspect must not choose the samples.
e: Hairs vary across the head, so several areas are sampled.

q: A farmer collapses after spraying pesticide. He has pinpoint pupils, heavy sweating and excessive salivation. Which antidote is used?
a: Atropine
Sodium thiosulfate
Naloxone
Vitamin K
r: These are signs of organophosphate poisoning, treated with atropine, often with pralidoxime.
Sodium thiosulfate is used in cyanide poisoning.
Naloxone reverses opioid overdose.
Vitamin K reverses certain anticoagulant poisonings.
e: Organophosphates inhibit cholinesterase, causing a buildup of acetylcholine.

q: A man is bitten by a cobra. What is the specific treatment for this biological poison?
a: Antivenin (antivenom)
Atropine
Activated charcoal
Sodium nitrite
r: Antivenin contains antibodies that neutralize the snake's venom.
Atropine treats organophosphate poisoning.
Activated charcoal binds ingested poisons in the gut, not injected venom.
Sodium nitrite is used in cyanide poisoning.
e: Biological poisons come from living things, such as venoms and bacterial toxins; chemical poisons are substances like cyanide and pesticides.

q: What is a document whose genuineness or authorship is disputed?
a: Questioned document
Standard document
Official document
Holographic document
r: A questioned document is any document whose source or authenticity is in question.
A standard is a known writing used for comparison.
An official document is issued by a public office; it may or may not be questioned.
A holographic document is written entirely by the hand of its author, such as a holographic will.
e: Questioned document examination compares questioned writings with known standards.

q: What are the known writings of a person, used for comparison with a questioned writing, called?
a: Standards or exemplars
Questioned writings
Disguised writings
Simulated writings
r: Standards (exemplars) are writings whose authorship is known.
Questioned writings are those under examination.
Disguised writings are deliberately altered by the writer.
Simulated writings are imitations of another person's writing.
e: Standards may be collected or requested.

q: Why are collected standards often preferred over requested standards?
a: They were written naturally, before any comparison was expected
They are always written with a ballpoint pen
They are written in front of the examiner
They are always newer than the questioned document
r: Collected standards come from ordinary business and personal writing, so they show natural habits without disguise.
The writing instrument varies.
Requested standards, not collected ones, are written in front of an investigator.
Standards should be close in date to the questioned writing, older or newer.
e: Requested standards help when collected ones are lacking, and allow the same text to be written.

q: What makes a document a public document rather than a private one?
a: It is an official act or record, or is acknowledged before a notary
It is written on expensive paper with a letterhead
It has been shown to many people
It was written by a famous person
r: Public documents include written official acts and records and notarized documents; others are private documents.
Paper and letterhead do not make a document public.
Publicity does not change the legal character of a document.
The fame of the writer is irrelevant.
e: The distinction matters for authentication under Rule 132.

q: Why is a stereoscopic microscope used in examining a questioned signature?
a: It gives a magnified 3-D view of strokes, pen lifts and retouching
It reads the invisible serial number printed in the paper
It measures the age of the ink in exact years
It removes the ink so the paper can be examined
r: The stereo microscope shows depth and detail of strokes, revealing hesitation, pen lifts and patching.
Paper does not have invisible serial numbers to be read this way.
No microscope can give the exact age of ink in years.
The microscope does not remove ink; examination is non-destructive.
e: Other equipment includes UV and IR light sources and the video spectral comparator.

q: Two signatures on different checks superimpose perfectly over each other. What does this suggest?
a: One is likely traced, since genuine signatures always vary naturally
Both are genuine, since they match exactly
Both are forged, since signatures should never match at all
Nothing, because superimposition has no meaning
r: No one signs exactly the same way twice; an exact match suggests tracing from a model.
Exact identity is a warning sign, not proof of genuineness.
Genuine signatures are similar but not identical; one may still be genuine.
Exact superimposition is significant evidence of tracing.
e: The model signature from which the tracing was made may be found among the genuine ones.

q: A questioned signature has blunt starts and ends, tremor, and pen lifts in odd places, while the standards are fluent with tapered strokes. What is the likely finding?
a: Simulated forgery
Genuine signature written in haste
Disguised writing by the owner
Simple forgery
r: Slow, drawn strokes, tremor and unnatural pen lifts are signs of a careful freehand copy.
Haste produces speed and fluency, not tremor and blunt strokes.
Disguise is the owner altering his own writing; the signs here point to copying.
Simple forgery makes no attempt to copy the genuine form.
e: Line quality is one of the most important indicators in signature examination.

q: A forger signed the account holder's name in his own ordinary handwriting without trying to copy the real signature. What type of forgery is this?
a: Simple (spurious) forgery
Simulated forgery
Traced forgery
Guided-hand signature
r: Simple forgery writes the name with no attempt to imitate the genuine signature.
Simulated forgery is a freehand copy of the genuine signature.
Traced forgery follows the outline of a genuine model.
A guided-hand signature is made with another person helping the writer's hand.
e: Simple forgeries are usually easy to detect when compared with standards.

q: Under magnification, faint carbon lines appear beneath the ink strokes of a questioned signature. What method of forgery was likely used?
a: Traced forgery using carbon paper
Simple forgery written freehand
Cut-and-paste of a genuine signature
Disguised writing by the owner
r: Carbon outlines under the ink show that the forger traced a model through carbon paper and then inked over it.
A freehand forgery leaves no carbon outline.
A cut-and-paste would show cut edges or a printed image, not carbon lines.
Disguised writing does not leave carbon outlines.
e: Indented-line tracing and transmitted-light tracing are other tracing methods.

q: Requested standards must be taken from a suspect. Which procedure is correct?
a: Dictate the text and remove each sample from view once written
Let him copy the questioned document word for word
Take only one sample so he does not get tired
Allow him to choose the pen and paper he likes
r: Dictation and removing each sample prevents the writer from copying or keeping his disguise consistent.
Copying the questioned document lets him imitate or avoid its features.
Several samples are needed to show natural variation.
Writing materials should be similar to those of the questioned document.
e: Samples should be taken under conditions similar to the questioned writing.

q: A writer deliberately changed his slant and made his letters larger so he would not be identified. What kind of writing is this?
a: Disguised writing
Simulated forgery
Traced forgery
Natural variation
r: Disguised writing is a deliberate change in one's own writing to avoid identification.
Simulated forgery imitates another person's writing.
Traced forgery follows a model's outline.
Natural variation is the normal, unintended differences in a person's writing.
e: Disguise is hard to keep up, so habitual features often still show.

q: The amount on a check appears to have been changed from 100 to 700. Which examination is most appropriate?
a: Examine it under ultraviolet and infrared light
Ask the bank teller whether the check looks correct
Compare the paper's weight with another check
Wet the check to see whether the ink runs
r: UV and IR examination can show inks that look the same but differ in composition, revealing alterations.
A teller's opinion is not a scientific examination.
Paper weight does not show an alteration of the figures.
Wetting can damage the evidence.
e: Non-destructive methods come first in document examination.

q: A questioned and a standard signature look alike in general form, but differ in how strokes begin, in pen pressure and in letter connections. How should the examiner weigh this?
a: Differences in habitual details matter more than similarity in general form
Similarity in general form is enough to declare them the same
Differences in details should be ignored as normal
Pen pressure is irrelevant in handwriting examination
r: A forger can copy the general form, but habitual details like stroke beginnings, pressure and connections are hard to imitate.
Pictorial similarity is what a forger aims for, so it proves little.
Fundamental differences in habits are significant, not normal variation.
Pressure patterns are among the habits examined.
e: Identification rests on significant writing habits, not on overall appearance.

q: Why is natural variation important in signature identification?
a: Genuine signatures vary slightly, so a lack of variation is suspicious
Natural variation proves that every signature is a forgery
Natural variation means no signature can ever be identified
Natural variation applies only to typewritten documents
r: The examiner must know the range of a writer's natural variation; differences within it are normal, and unnatural sameness is suspicious.
Variation is expected in genuine writing.
Identification is possible by comparing questioned writing with the range shown by enough standards.
Variation is a feature of handwriting, not typewriting.
e: This is why several standards, not one, are needed for comparison.

q: A suspected banknote feels flat and smooth, and no portrait watermark appears when it is held against the light. What does this suggest?
a: It is likely counterfeit, because genuine notes have raised print and a watermark
It is genuine, because worn notes always lose their raised print
It is genuine, because watermarks are seen only under ultraviolet light
Nothing, because the feel and watermark are not security features
r: Genuine notes are printed by intaglio, which feels raised, and carry a watermark visible against light.
Wear can reduce texture, but a missing watermark cannot be explained by wear.
Watermarks are seen with transmitted light, not only under UV.
Both are important security features of genuine notes.
e: Suspected counterfeits are referred to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas for examination.

q: Why should a counterfeit examination check several security features instead of only one?
a: Counterfeiters may copy one feature, but copying all of them is far harder
One feature is always enough to prove a note is genuine
Checking several features damages the banknote
Only the serial number matters in counterfeit detection
r: Banknotes use layered features such as watermark, security thread, color-shifting ink and intaglio print; a fake rarely copies all of them well.
A single imitated feature can mislead.
Visual and tactile checks do not damage notes.
Serial numbers are easy to print and are not the main test.
e: The feel-look-tilt method is commonly taught for checking banknotes.

q: Who developed, in 1921, the instrument that continuously recorded blood pressure, pulse and breathing to detect deception?
a: John A. Larson
Leonarde Keeler
Cesare Lombroso
William M. Marston
r: John Larson, a police officer and physiologist in Berkeley, developed the first modern polygraph in 1921.
Leonarde Keeler later improved the polygraph and added the galvanograph.
Lombroso used a hydrosphygmograph to measure blood pressure changes in 1895.
Marston developed the systolic blood pressure deception test.
e: Keeler's improvements made the polygraph portable and more widely used.

q: What does the galvanograph component of the polygraph record?
a: Changes in the skin's electrical conductance
Changes in breathing rate and depth
Changes in blood pressure and pulse
Movements of the subject's body
r: The galvanograph (electrodermal) component records changes in skin conductance linked to sweat gland activity.
Breathing is recorded by the pneumograph.
Blood pressure and pulse are recorded by the cardiosphygmograph.
Body movements are recorded by motion sensors.
e: Each component records a different physiological response.

q: Why can extreme nervousness in an innocent subject affect the accuracy of a polygraph test?
a: It may cause reactions that look like deception, giving a false result
It makes the polygraph instrument stop working
It always makes a guilty person look innocent
It has no effect, because the polygraph measures only lies
r: Fear and nervousness produce physiological reactions that can be mistaken for deception; the pretest interview aims to reduce this.
Nervousness does not stop the instrument.
Nervousness can affect both innocent and guilty subjects in various ways.
The polygraph measures physiological responses, not lies directly.
e: Factors affecting accuracy include the subject's condition, the examiner's skill and the test environment.

q: Why should a subject be rested, fed and free from drugs before a polygraph test?
a: Fatigue, hunger or drugs can alter physiological responses
The subject's appetite is part of the test questions
Drugs make the subject tell the truth automatically
Resting is needed only for tests done at night
r: The polygraph records physiological changes, so anything that alters them, like fatigue or drugs, can affect accuracy.
Appetite is not part of the questions.
No drug forces truthfulness; drugs can suppress or exaggerate reactions.
The subject's condition matters at any time of day.
e: Examiners check the subject's physical and mental fitness during the pretest.

q: The examiner explains the instrument, discusses the case and reviews every question with the subject before attaching the sensors. Which phase is this?
a: Pre-test interview
In-test (chart recording)
Post-test interview
Chart interpretation
r: The pretest interview prepares the subject, reviews the questions and builds understanding before recording.
The in-test phase is the actual recording of charts.
The post-test phase follows the recording.
Interpretation is the analysis of the charts.
e: Reviewing the questions avoids surprise reactions to unfamiliar wording.

q: After the charts show significant reactions, the examiner discusses the results with the subject and invites an explanation. Which phase is this?
a: Post-test interview
Pre-test interview
In-test (chart recording)
Instrument calibration
r: The post-test interview follows the recording and gives the subject a chance to explain reactions.
The pretest comes before recording.
The in-test phase is the recording itself.
Calibration is a technical check of the instrument.
e: Admissions made during the post-test must follow the subject's constitutional rights.

q: Which polygraph component uses rubber tubes placed around the chest and abdomen?
a: Pneumograph
Cardiosphygmograph
Galvanograph
Kymograph
r: The pneumograph records breathing through tubes around the chest and abdomen.
The cardiosphygmograph uses a cuff to record blood pressure and pulse.
The galvanograph uses electrodes on the fingers.
The kymograph moves the chart paper in analog instruments.
e: Both thoracic and abdominal breathing are recorded.

q: Which polygraph component uses a blood pressure cuff on the subject's upper arm?
a: Cardiosphygmograph
Pneumograph
Galvanograph
Motion sensor
r: The cardiosphygmograph records changes in relative blood pressure and pulse through the arm cuff.
The pneumograph records breathing.
The galvanograph records skin conductance.
A motion sensor records body movements.
e: The cuff is inflated to a moderate pressure during each chart.

q: Which polygraph component uses electrodes attached to two of the subject's fingers?
a: Galvanograph
Pneumograph
Cardiosphygmograph
Kymograph
r: The galvanograph uses finger electrodes to measure skin conductance.
The pneumograph uses chest and abdominal tubes.
The cardiosphygmograph uses an arm cuff.
The kymograph is the chart drive.
e: Electrodermal responses are among the most sensitive polygraph measures.

q: A reaction appears on a relevant question in only one of three charts. How should it be treated?
a: As unreliable, because meaningful reactions should be consistent across charts
As conclusive proof that the subject lied
As a reason to stop the test and arrest the subject
As a sign that the subject is telling the truth on all questions
r: Chart interpretation relies on consistent reactions across repeated charts, not a single reaction.
One reaction is not proof of deception.
No arrest can be based on a single chart reaction.
An isolated reaction does not prove truthfulness either.
e: Repeating the questions in several charts helps separate real reactions from chance ones.

q: The subject coughs just as a relevant question is asked. What should the examiner do?
a: Mark the cough, disregard that reaction and repeat the question
Treat the reaction as a clear sign of deception
Stop the examination permanently
Erase the part of the chart that shows the cough
r: Movements and coughs distort the tracings, so they are marked, the reaction is not scored, and the question is repeated.
A cough is an artifact, not evidence of deception.
A cough does not require ending the test.
Charts must not be erased or altered.
e: Marking artifacts keeps the chart an accurate record.

q: How should polygraph results be regarded in Philippine courts?
a: As investigative aids, not as conclusive evidence of guilt or innocence
As conclusive proof of guilt whenever deception is indicated
As sufficient to convict without any other evidence
As evidence that must be accepted if the examiner is licensed
r: The Supreme Court has treated polygraph results as lacking general scientific acceptance as proof of guilt or innocence; they guide investigation.
Courts do not treat polygraph results as conclusive.
A conviction requires proof beyond reasonable doubt from competent evidence.
The examiner's license does not make the results binding on the court.
e: The polygraph is useful in narrowing leads and obtaining admissions made with proper safeguards.

q: A subject reacts consistently more to the relevant questions than to the comparison (control) questions. How is this interpreted?
a: It indicates deception on the relevant issue
It indicates truthfulness on the relevant issue
It shows the comparison questions were badly worded
It shows that the instrument is broken
r: In comparison question tests, greater reactions to relevant than to comparison questions indicate deception.
Truthful subjects tend to react more to the comparison questions.
Consistent results do not by themselves show poor wording.
Consistent patterns show the instrument is recording.
e: Comparison questions are designed to concern truthful subjects more than the relevant questions do.

q: What is the purpose of irrelevant questions such as 'Are you sitting down?' in a polygraph test?
a: To set a baseline of normal responses and allow recovery between questions
To trap the subject into lying about the crime
To make the subject nervous before the relevant questions
To test whether the subject understands the language
r: Irrelevant questions produce normal responses used as a baseline, and they give the subject time to return to normal.
Irrelevant questions are not traps.
They are meant to settle, not unsettle, the subject.
Language is checked in the pretest, not by irrelevant questions.
e: The three types of questions are relevant, irrelevant and comparison (control).

q: Which instrument lets an examiner view two bullets side by side in one field of view?
a: Comparison microscope
Stereoscopic microscope
Helixometer
Bullet recovery box
r: The comparison microscope joins two microscopes by an optical bridge so two objects are seen in one split view.
The stereo microscope gives a 3-D view of a single object.
The helixometer measures the pitch of rifling.
The bullet recovery box catches test bullets.
e: The comparison microscope is the main instrument for identifying fired bullets and cartridge cases.

q: Why are test bullets fired into a water tank or cotton-filled box?
a: To recover them undamaged so their marks can be compared
To measure the loudness of the gunshot
To clean the barrel of the suspect firearm
To find out the age of the ammunition
r: Water tanks and cotton boxes slow the bullet gently, keeping its striations intact for comparison.
These devices are not used to measure sound.
Test firing does not clean the barrel.
Recovery devices do not date ammunition.
e: Test bullets from the suspect firearm are compared with the evidence bullet.

q: What does a firearms examiner measure with a helixometer?
a: The pitch or twist of the rifling in the barrel
The weight of a fired bullet
The pressure of the gas inside the chamber
The distance of the shooter from the target
r: The helixometer measures the pitch of rifling, a class characteristic of the firearm.
Bullet weight is measured with a balance.
Chamber pressure is measured with special pressure gauges.
Firing distance is estimated from powder patterns.
e: Class characteristics such as twist help narrow the possible firearms.

q: Why should a bullet embedded in a wall not be pried out with a knife?
a: The knife may scratch it and destroy the marks needed for comparison
The bullet may explode if touched by metal
The wall will become weaker and collapse
The bullet must remain in the wall until the trial is over
r: Prying can add marks that obscure the striations; the material around the bullet should be cut away instead.
A fired bullet does not explode.
The concern is the evidence, not the wall's strength.
The bullet is recovered for examination; photographs record its position.
e: Careful recovery protects the individual characteristics on the bullet.

q: How should a firearms examiner support his conclusion when testifying in court?
a: By explaining the comparison and showing photomicrographs of the matching marks
By stating only that he is an expert and is certain
By asking the judge to examine the bullets without explanation
By relying on the suspect's admission instead of the examination
r: Expert testimony should explain the basis of the opinion; photomicrographs let the court see the agreement of marks.
An expert's opinion is weighed by its basis, not by the expert's say-so.
The examiner must explain the findings to help the court.
The examination stands on its own scientific basis.
e: Courts evaluate expert opinion by the reasons and methods given.
l: Rules of Court, Rule 130, Sec. 52 (opinion of expert witness)

q: What is the role of the Integrated Ballistics Identification System (IBIS)?
a: It compares digital images of fired bullets and cases to suggest possible matches
It replaces the examiner and gives the final identification
It test-fires guns automatically without ammunition
It traces the owner of a gun through its serial number
r: IBIS correlates images in a database to find candidates, which an examiner then confirms with the comparison microscope.
The system suggests candidates; the examiner makes the identification.
Test firing still requires ammunition.
Serial number tracing is done through firearms registration records.
e: Ballistic databases help link shootings across different cases.

q: Which branch of ballistics studies a bullet's flight from the muzzle to the target, including gravity and air resistance?
a: Exterior ballistics
Interior ballistics
Terminal ballistics
Forensic ballistics
r: Exterior ballistics covers the projectile's motion after it leaves the muzzle.
Interior ballistics covers events inside the firearm.
Terminal ballistics covers the effect on the target.
Forensic ballistics applies ballistics to legal questions.
e: The branches follow the stages of a bullet's journey.

q: A study examines how a bullet penetrates and wounds the body. Which branch of ballistics is this?
a: Terminal ballistics
Exterior ballistics
Interior ballistics
Shot ballistics
r: Terminal ballistics deals with the bullet's effect when it strikes its target.
Exterior ballistics deals with flight.
Interior ballistics deals with events inside the firearm.
There is no standard branch called shot ballistics.
e: Wound ballistics is a part of terminal ballistics.

q: Which branch of ballistics covers events from the firing pin's strike on the primer until the bullet leaves the muzzle?
a: Interior ballistics
Exterior ballistics
Terminal ballistics
Wound ballistics
r: Interior ballistics covers ignition, burning of the propellant and the bullet's travel through the barrel.
Exterior ballistics begins at the muzzle.
Terminal ballistics concerns the target.
Wound ballistics concerns injuries to the body.
e: Rifling marks are made on the bullet during the interior ballistic stage.

q: A firearm with no rifling in its barrel fires many small pellets with each shot. How is it classified?
a: Smoothbore firearm (shotgun)
Rifled long firearm (rifle)
Machine pistol
Revolver
r: Shotguns have smooth bores and usually fire multiple pellets.
Rifled firearms have lands and grooves.
A machine pistol is a rifled automatic handgun.
A revolver is a rifled handgun with a revolving cylinder.
e: Firearms are classified by bore as smoothbore or rifled.

q: An evidence bullet shows six lands and grooves with a left twist. The suspect's gun has five lands and grooves with a right twist. What should be concluded?
a: The bullet was not fired from the suspect's gun
The bullet was fired from the suspect's gun
The comparison is inconclusive and must be repeated
The bullet was fired from a shotgun
r: Different class characteristics, the number of lands and direction of twist, exclude the firearm.
A firearm cannot leave class characteristics different from its own barrel.
Differences in class characteristics are clear enough to exclude.
Shotguns do not leave land and groove marks.
e: Class characteristics can exclude a firearm; individual characteristics are needed to identify one.

q: Which part of a cartridge is struck by the firing pin to ignite the propellant?
a: Primer
Bullet
Cartridge case mouth
Gunpowder
r: The primer contains a sensitive compound that explodes when struck, igniting the powder.
The bullet is the projectile.
The mouth of the case holds the bullet.
Gunpowder is ignited by the primer, not struck directly.
e: The parts of a cartridge are the bullet, cartridge case, propellant and primer.

q: What does the gauge number of a 12-gauge shotgun mean?
a: The bore fits a lead ball weighing 1/12 of a pound
The bore is 12 millimeters in diameter
The barrel is 12 inches long
The gun holds 12 shells
r: Gauge is the number of lead balls of the bore's diameter that make one pound; 12 balls of a 12-gauge bore weigh one pound.
Gauge is not measured in millimeters.
Gauge does not refer to barrel length.
Gauge does not refer to magazine capacity.
e: The higher the gauge number, the smaller the bore, except the .410, which is a caliber.

q: Two bullets have the same caliber, number of lands and twist, and their fine striations line up under the comparison microscope. What can be concluded?
a: They were fired from the same firearm
They were fired from two different firearms
They came from the same box of ammunition
They were fired on the same day
r: Agreement of individual characteristics, the striations, identifies a single firearm.
Agreeing striations exclude different firearms.
Striations come from the barrel, not from the ammunition box.
The marks do not show the date of firing.
e: Individual characteristics come from tiny, random imperfections in the barrel.

q: Only a fired cartridge case was found at the scene, and no bullet. Can it be linked to a particular firearm?
a: Yes, through firing pin, breech face, extractor and ejector marks
No, because only bullets carry identifying marks
No, because cartridge cases are never marked by the firearm
Yes, but only by reading its brand stamped on the head
r: The firearm's parts leave individual marks on the case, which can be compared with test-fired cases.
Cartridge cases also carry identifying marks.
Firing pins, breech faces and extractors mark the case.
The headstamp shows the maker, not the firearm.
e: Cartridge cases are often the only ballistic evidence left by semi-automatic firearms.

q: An examiner finds that the class characteristics of the evidence bullet and the test bullets agree, but the striations are too damaged to compare. What is the best conclusion?
a: Inconclusive: the gun can be neither identified nor excluded
Identification: the bullet was fired from the suspect's gun
Exclusion: the bullet was not fired from the suspect's gun
Identification, because class characteristics are enough
r: Agreement in class characteristics without enough individual detail allows neither identification nor exclusion.
An identification needs sufficient agreement of individual marks.
Agreeing class characteristics do not support exclusion.
Many firearms share the same class characteristics.
e: Reporting limits honestly is part of sound forensic practice.

q: Where should an investigator put his identifying mark on a recovered bullet?
a: On the base or nose, never on the sides with rifling marks
On the sides, where the rifling marks are clearest
On any part, since marks do not affect the examination
On the sides, after first scraping them clean
r: Marking the base or nose avoids damaging the striations on the bearing surface.
Marking the sides destroys the evidence needed for comparison.
Marks on the wrong part can ruin the comparison.
Scraping destroys the striations.
e: Some laboratories prefer marking the container instead of the bullet itself.

q: Why should a firearm at a crime scene not be picked up by putting a pencil into its barrel?
a: It can damage the barrel and disturb trace evidence inside it
It may cause the firearm to be classified wrongly
It makes the serial number harder to read
It is too slow when there are many firearms
r: Inserting objects into the barrel can scratch it, alter marks and disturb residue or blood inside.
Classification does not depend on how the gun is picked up.
Picking it up by the barrel does not affect the serial number.
The issue is preservation of evidence, not speed.
e: Firearms are handled by the edges of the grip or checkered areas, after making them safe.

q: Why is a fired cartridge case marked inside its mouth rather than on its head?
a: The head bears the firing pin and breech face marks
The mouth is the only part made of brass
Marks on the head make the case explode
The head must be kept clean for fingerprints only
r: Marks on the head could obliterate the firing pin, breech face, extractor and ejector marks.
The case is usually brass throughout.
A fired case does not explode.
The head carries ballistic marks, which is the main reason to keep it unmarked.
e: The mark is placed where it will not interfere with the examination.

q: Why is each recovered bullet wrapped separately in soft tissue and placed in its own small box?
a: To keep the striations from rubbing and the items from mixing
To keep the bullets warm until examination
To make them lighter to carry to the laboratory
To allow the bullets to dry in the open air
r: Separate, padded packaging prevents damage to marks and keeps each item's identity.
Temperature does not affect bullets.
Weight is not the reason for packaging.
Bullets are protected in closed containers, not left in the open.
e: Each container is sealed and labeled for the chain of custody.

q: An examiner must write the conclusion of a bullet comparison report for court. Which formulation is best?
a: 'Evidence bullet EB-1 and the test bullets were fired from the submitted pistol, based on agreeing striations.'
'I am one hundred percent sure that no other gun in the world could have fired it.'
'The suspect is guilty of the shooting because the bullet came from his gun.'
'The bullets seem quite similar, and the gun might possibly be the one.'
r: A good conclusion is clear and objective: it names the items, states the result and gives its basis.
Claims of absolute certainty go beyond what the science supports.
Guilt is for the court to decide, not the examiner.
Vague wording does not state a clear finding.
e: A forensic report usually states the request, the items received, the examinations done, the findings and the conclusion.

q: A laboratory analyst spills a strong acid on her forearm. What is the correct first aid?
a: Flush the area with plenty of running water for at least 15 minutes
Cover the area with a dry cloth and wait for help
Neutralize it at once by pouring a strong base on it
Apply butter or oil to soothe the skin
r: Immediate, prolonged flushing with water removes and dilutes the chemical.
Waiting lets the acid keep burning.
A strong base causes a heat-producing reaction and more injury.
Butter or oil traps the chemical and heat on the skin.
e: Laboratories must have safety showers, eyewash stations and safety data sheets for chemicals.
